title: FlAsH-ID enables live-cell photoproximity labeling with a short peptide tag.
abstract: Proximity labeling has emerged as a valuable tool for the interrogation of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions. Almost all proximity labeling methods are deployed using large fusion proteins, which, while powerful in many contexts, can disrupt native biology or obscure important epitopes on the protein under study. Here we develop a photoproximity labeling method that is localized to a short 6-aa peptide sequence. Termed FlAsH-ID, this method uses the combination of the Tsien tetracysteine tag with the FlAsH dye for localized singlet oxygen generation. We demonstrate that this green-light-based method is nontoxic and can be used to label proteins within several cellular compartments. Lastly, we establish that FlAsH-ID can be deployed in primary CD8+ T cells to assess the interactome of the transcription factor RUNX3. Our results suggest this technique will expand the field of proximity labeling to small, functionally sensitive proteins in primary cells without perturbing their function.

title: Dissecting the transcriptome of Parkin (PRKN)-linked Parkinson's disease using 2D and 3D hiPSC-neuronal models.
abstract: Mutations in the Parkin (PRKN) gene are the most common known cause of autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease (PD), and Parkin dysfunction represents a risk factor for idiopathic PD. Parkin is an E3 ubiquitin ligase, involved in protein quality control and the removal of damaged mitochondria. Here, we generate human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons using both a 2D differentiation protocol and our recently developed 3D method based on the microencapsulation of hiPSCs in small alginate/fibronectin beads. The transcriptional signature of cells from PD patients carrying PRKN mutations is evaluated at the neuronal stage and during the differentiation process. Analyses of mutation-specific gene sets and associated pathways reveal multiple biological processes implicated in PRKN-pathology, including synaptic and metabolic function, inflammation, and intracellular trafficking, reflecting a layered disease development. These data map the contribution of Parkin in early PD pathogenesis and progression before overt neurodegeneration.

title: Observational in vivo axon development during early childhood in autism spectrum disorder and developmental disability using MRI.
abstract: Elucidating the altered spatiotemporal development of white matter (WM) axons during early childhood is essential for uncovering the neuropathology of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, previous studies have often failed to account for the heterogeneity of developmental trajectories or to adequately control for co-occurring developmental delay/intellectual disability (DD/ID), limiting our understanding of whether ASD-related alterations represent qualitative deviations or quantitative delays in otherwise preserved maturational patterns. We analyzed multi-shell diffusion MRI and behavioral data from 364 children aged 1-7 years (156 individuals with ASD, 48 individuals with DD/ID, and 160 typically developing (TD) controls) using the Neurite Density Index (NDI)-an MRI-derived marker of axonal density. A subset of ASD children also underwent longitudinal MRI scans and provided blood metabolic and protein profiles. We identified the same three WM clusters in both typical and atypical development. These clusters exhibit distinct developmental stages with successively decreasing growth rates in ASD, similar to TD but delayed overall, especially for ASD with DD/ID, while DD/ID display little developmental effect. These findings are further validated across split-half, male-only and longitudinal subdatasets. Furthermore, we found NDIs of these WM clusters in ASD are: a) correlated with cognitive impairments at the stage with a fast developmental pace and social deficits at the stage with a moderate-slow developmental pace; b) linked with multiple metabolic and protein measurements. ASD children exhibit the same coordinated spatial pattern of white matter development as TD, but with distinct developmental trajectories. These findings advance our understanding of the neuropathological underpinnings of ASD heterogeneity in early childhood, and highlight potential targets for future therapeutic design and evaluation.

title: Pharmacological chaperone treatment with Cystadane in aspartylglucosaminuria: an open-label, phase Ib/II trial.
abstract: This phase Ib/II investigator-initiated, open label trial aims to show the safety and efficacy of Cystadane (betaine) in aspartylglucosaminuria, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, in Finnish patients homozygous for the Finnish major mutation, aged between 3 and 17 years at study begin (recruited: 25, analyzed: 21). Oral Cystadane efficacy and safety were studied over 48 months. The primary endpoint of the study, reduction of glycoasparagines in the urine, was quantitatively determined using liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry and normalized to urine creatinine. Urine glycoasparagines are significantly reduced upon Cystadane treatment (by 68.6% ±10.8%; p = 0.000), and the study thus meets its primary endpoint. Our data show that Cystadane/betaine efficiently improves the main disease biomarker, and it is safe to use in aspartylglucosaminuria. Further studies should be carried out in a larger patient population over a longer time to demonstrate the effects on disease progression. EudraCT registration number 2017-000645-48.

title: Posterior-lateral basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei hypoconnectivity in the inferior frontal cortex is associated with verbal fluency deficits in schizophrenia.
abstract: Cognitive impairment is a core feature of schizophrenia and remains insufficiently addressed by current treatments. Increasing evidence implicates the cholinergic system, particularly the basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei (BFCN), in cognitive dysfunction. While structural alterations of the BFCN have been reported, alterations in their intrinsic functional connectivity (iFC) remain unclear. The present study examined the iFC of anterior and posterior BFCN subdivisions (aBFCN, pBFCN) in schizophrenia and tested associations with cognitive performance. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from the COBRE dataset were analyzed, including 73 healthy controls (HC) and 51 patients with schizophrenia (SCZ). Seed-based connectivity analyses were performed for aBFCN and pBFCN. Group differences were assessed voxel-wise, and group-dependent associations with phonemic verbal fluency (FAS) and processing speed (BACS-SC) were tested using hierarchical regression controlling for age, sex, IQ, and smoking status; verbal learning and memory (HVLT) was examined as a specificity analysis. Exploratory molecular mapping used normative PET-derived neurotransmitter maps, supplemented by spatial-autocorrelation-preserving null models. Distinct connectivity patterns of aBFCN and pBFCN were observed, consistent with previous reports in HC. Compared with HC, SCZ showed reduced pBFCN connectivity with a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus (pars opercularis; BA44; p = 0.018, FWE-corrected), whereas no significant differences were observed for aBFCN. The Group × pBFCN-IFG connectivity interaction was significant for FAS (p = 0.014) but not BACS-SC (p = 0.762) or HVLT (p = 0.514). In SCZ, higher pBFCN-IFG connectivity was associated with better FAS performance. Descriptive molecular mapping showed above-average representation of M1 and α4β2 receptor maps as well as several non-cholinergic targets; however, no molecular target showed significant spatial correspondence after spatial-autocorrelation-aware testing and FDR correction. These findings provide evidence for selective pBFCN hypoconnectivity with the right inferior frontal gyrus in schizophrenia. Its association with verbal fluency suggests that disrupted pBFCN connectivity with the inferior frontal cortex may contribute to altered executive control processes involved in verbal fluency in schizophrenia. Together, these findings extend previous evidence of BFCN abnormalities in schizophrenia by demonstrating a systems-level functional alteration of pBFCN-cortical connectivity and its relationship with cognitive performance.

title: Experience modifies the synaptome architecture in the developing and adult mouse brain.
abstract: Synaptome architecture describes the spatiotemporal distribution of highly diverse excitatory synapses throughout the brain. Whether and how this architecture is impacted by experience and sensory input is unknown. We found that environmental enrichment and monocular visual deprivation drive large-scale reconfiguration of excitatory synapse populations in more than one hundred regions of the mouse brain. Different experiences modify distinct subsets of synapse types and subtypes, with patterns aligned with protein turnover rates and connectome architecture. Similarity in experience-dependent reconfiguration during development and adulthood indicates shared mechanisms of synaptome adaptation across the lifespan. Our findings support a population-selection model in which experiences drive adaptation by selectively modifying synapse types and subtypes distributed across the brain. Experience-driven reconfiguration of synaptome architecture shares features with the response to aging, sleep deprivation, brain injury and genetic mutations, supporting a unifying principle of brain adaptation.

title: Elevated prenatal IL-6 levels disrupt early patterns of hippocampal electrical activity and chloride homeostasis by targeting GABAergic signaling at perinatal stage.
abstract: Early patterns of neuronal electrical activity are fundamental for driving critical developmental processes, including neuronal maturation and synapse formation. While genetic programs are key in orchestrating these events, the influence of environmental stressors remains poorly defined. Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy induces a systemic cytokine surge that can profoundly impact fetal brain development, increasing the risk of psychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. Here, we show that maternal elevation of interleukin-6 (IL-6) - a key cytokine upregulated during MIA - perturbs early hippocampal electrical activity in male offspring during the first postnatal week, a critical window for circuit formation. By triggering a STAT3-dependent modulation of early GABAergic synaptic transmission, IL-6 disrupts chloride homeostasis, causing a premature shift in the developmental GABA polarity switch. Our findings reveal a direct link between maternal immune signaling and early GABA-driven network maturation, providing insights into how inflammatory events during pregnancy may predispose male offspring to neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: The claustrum contributes to working memory maintenance in mice.
abstract: Working memory (WM) enables the temporary maintenance and manipulation of sensory information to guide behavior, yet the neural circuits supporting this process remain incompletely defined. The claustrum is a highly interconnected brain structure positioned to integrate distributed cortical activity, but its contribution to WM has remained unclear. Here, we combined microendoscopic calcium imaging, chemogenetic and optogenetic manipulations in mice performing sensory-guided WM tasks to examine the role of the claustrum in WM. Claustrum neurons exhibited cue-evoked activity that persisted across delay periods and evolved dynamically over time, with population states retaining information about cue identity on single trials. Reducing claustrum excitability during encoding, delay maintenance, or target comparison similarly impaired WM performance across sensory modalities, without affecting sensory processing, motor output, arousal or inhibitory control. Together, these findings reveal an important causal contribution of the claustrum to WM maintenance.

title: Association of pre-clinical depressive symptoms and its plasma metabolomic signature with Parkinson's disease: a community-based longitudinal study.
abstract: Accumulating evidence has suggested that depression is associated with an increased risk of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet whether pre-clinical depressive symptoms in PD development and the potential mediating effects of metabolomic profiles remain unclear. We aimed to examine the association between depressive symptoms and PD risk, evaluate effect modification by genetic susceptibility, and assess metabolomic mediation. This prospective study included 451,922 PD-free participants from the UK Biobank. Depressive symptoms were collected by a 2-item Patient Health Questionnaire (range, 0-6; ≥3 indicates possible depressive disorder) at baseline. Identification of PD was based on medical records. PD-related polygenic risk score (PRSPD), which incorporates established genes for PD based on external GWAS meta-analyses, was tertiled as low, moderate, and high. Baseline plasma metabolites were quantified via NMR spectroscopy from blood samples. Data were analyzed using Cox regression. Over a median follow-up of 14.6 years, 3108 (0.7%) participants developed PD. Higher depressive symptom severity showed linear association with PD risk (hazard ratio [HR]: 1.11, 95% confidence interval: 1.07-1.15). Participants with possible depressive disorder had 36% higher PD risk (HR: 1.36, 1.15-1.61). Those with both possible depressive disorder and high genetic risk had the highest PD risk (HR 2.15, 1.74-2.65; P for interaction = 0.028). Metabolomic signature, incorporating fatty acids and lipoproteins, accounted for 15% (model-based proportion) of the depressive symptoms-PD association. Pre-clinical depressive symptoms are associated with a moderately increased risk of PD, particularly among people with a high genetic susceptibility to PD. Metabolomic profiles account for a significant portion of this relationship.

title: Delayed brain network energy development in preterm youth impairs cognitive function: evidence from the longitudinal ABCD study.
abstract: Preterm birth disrupts early brain development, increasing the risk of cognitive difficulties. However, its long-term effects on functional brain network energy, a metric of large-scale network stability and adaptability, remain poorly understood. Using resting-state fMRI data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, we examined how prematurity influences brain network energy across late childhood and early adolescence. Our sample included 818 preterm-born youth and 2,149 matched full-term controls. Compared to full-term adolescents, preterm individuals exhibited altered multiscale functional connectivity and persistent reductions in functional network energy, specifically within the sensorimotor (SM) and higher-cognitive temporoparietal (HC-TP) networks, at both baseline and 2-year follow-up. These findings suggest diminished functional flexibility and network integration in preterm-born individuals. To further contextualize these results, we incorporated data from 1,633 participants in the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and HCP-Development studies, confirming that network energy increases with age in typically developing youth and is consistently reduced in preterm individuals. Notably, lower energy in the HC-TP network was specifically associated with deficits in crystallized cognition, but not with behavioral problems. Meta-analytic decoding further linked the HC-TP network to language and social cognition, providing a mechanistic explanation for its relationship with crystallized cognitive abilities. These findings highlight the persistence of neurodevelopmental alterations in preterm individuals, particularly affecting higher-order cognitive functions, and position network energy as a potential marker of altered neurodevelopment following preterm birth.

title: Levistilide A promotes ferroptosis through the RNF40-HSP90α axis and inhibit colorectal cancer lung metastasis.
abstract: The molecular mechanisms underlying lung metastasis of colorectal cancer (CRC) remain largely elusive, and effective therapeutic agents are still lacking. In this study, we identify levistilide A (LeA) as a potential anti-metastatic agent against CRC lung metastasis. We demonstrate that heat shock protein 90α (HSP90α) is markedly upregulated in CRC and promotes lung metastasis by suppressing ferroptosis. Notably, combined treatment with LeA and the ferroptosis inducer RSL3 further alleviates lung metastatic burden in vivo. Mechanistically, we reveal that the E3 ubiquitin ligase ring finger protein 40 (RNF40) suppresses CRC cell proliferation by directly interacting with HSP90α, inducing ubiquitination at lysine 407 and promoting its proteasomal degradation. RNF40-mediated HSP90α downregulation leads to the accumulation of malondialdehyde (MDA) and reactive oxygen species (ROS), thereby inhibiting CRC cell growth. Collectively, our findings provide mechanistic insights into how LeA directly targets HSP90α or facilitates RNF40-HSP90α-mediated degradation of HSP90α to regulate ferroptosis in CRC.

title: A single-nucleus multiome map of the human cerebellum with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias.
abstract: Although cerebellum is neuropathologically affected in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and AD-related dementia (ADRD), the cell type-specific genomic and epigenomic changes remain poorly understood. Here, we present single-nucleus multiome (RNA-seq and ATAC-seq) analysis of 103,861 nuclei isolated from both the cerebellum and frontal cortex of diseased individuals and cognitively healthy controls. We identify 431,834 significant peak-to-gene linkages across cell subtypes, revealing cis-regulatory elements linked to cell type-specific and disease-associated transcriptomic and regulatory network changes. Differential trajectory analysis pinpoints disease-associated genes in cerebellar granule cells, such as STMN1 and CLU. Integrating epigenomic, genetic, and three-dimensional genome data, we pinpoint two likely causal variants linked to SEZ6L2 in Purkinje cells and KANSL1 in granule cells. Through CRISPR interference in patient-derived cerebellar organoids, we show that silencing the variant-containing regulatory elements suppresses SEZ6L2 and KANSL1 expression, which perturbs neurodegeneration-associated gene programs. This cell type-specific regulatory landscape provides genomic and epigenomic insights into the pathological role of the cerebellum in AD/ADRD.

title: Targeting peripheral cathepsin E restricts CD8+ T-cell neuroinvasion and ameliorates Alzheimer's disease pathology.
journal: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
abstract: CD8+ T-cell-mediated neuroimmune activation increases with aging and contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular cues that drive their recruitment into the brain remain largely undefined. We quantified Cathepsin E (CatE) expression in CD8+ T cells from 5×FAD mice and clinical samples from patients with AD. The functional necessity of CatE in T-cell trafficking was assessed through 4D-data-independent acquisition (4D-DIA) proteomics, microfluidic migration assays under physiological flow, and adoptive transfer experiments. Finally, we evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of a brain-impermeable CatE inhibitor in mitigating AD-related pathology. CatE is selectively and age-dependently upregulated in peripheral CD8+ T cells in both AD mice and patients. Adoptive transfer of AD-derived CD8+ T cells significantly accelerated promoted soluble Aβ₁- 4 2 accumulation, glial activation, and memory deficits in 5-month-old recipient mice. Mechanistically, CatE is associated with elevated expression of vinculin and fibronectin in CD8+ T cells, accompanied by enhanced activation of β1-integrins that stabilizes adhesion to brain endothelial cells. Pharmacological suppression of peripheral CatE effectively restricted T-cell infiltration, attenuated neuroinflammation, and restored cognitive function in AD models. These results identify CatE as a key cell-intrinsic regulator of CD8+ T-cell migratory competence. Targeting the peripheral CatE-integrin axis offers a promising immunotherapeutic strategy to limit pathogenic neuroinflammation in AD while circumventing the challenges of blood-brain barrier penetration.

title: The Cylinder Test: Development and clinical validation of a tool for assessing hand opening.
journal: Journal of hand therapy : official journal of the American Society of Hand Therapists
abstract: Impaired hand opening following neurological injury can limit functional grasp and object handling. Existing upper limb assessments do not specifically evaluate functional hand opening or distinguish between active and passive components. To describe the development of the Cylinder Test (CyT) and evaluate its preliminary face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance among clinicians and individuals with neurological upper limb impairment. Clinical measurement, cross-sectional study. The CyT was developed through iterative clinical refinement and literature review. The final CyT version comprises 14 plastic cylinders (20-150 mm diameter) and four subtests assessing active and passive functional hand opening. Face validity was evaluated in 33 individuals with neurological upper limb impairments due to cervical spinal cord injuries (cSCI) or spasticity and 31 clinicians experienced in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. Clinicians reviewed the CyT manual and completed a study-specific questionnaire assessing clarity, perceived clinical usefulness, relevance of the subtests, and scoring criteria. Participants performed the CyT and subsequently rated its relevance and perceived effort. Data were summarized descriptively. All clinicians (31/31, 100%) reported that the manual provided sufficient guidance for independent administration, and all considered the CyT potentially useful in clinical practice. The purpose of the CyT was rated as clear or very clear by 26/31 clinicians (84%), and no clinician rated any subtest or scoring criterion as inappropriate. All participants (33/33, 100%) rated the overall CyT as relevant or very relevant, and ratings of the individual subtests were predominantly relevant or very relevant. Six of 15 participants with spasticity rated the test as demanding compared with 2/18 participants with cSCI. Preliminary evaluation supports the face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance of the CyT for assessing functional hand opening in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. The CyT may provide hand therapists with a clinically feasible approach to assessing active and passive hand opening. Further evaluation of reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness is required.

title: Effects of Cerebellar and Primary Motor Cortex tDCS Montages on Vocal Performance in Singers: A Randomized Trial.
authors: Silva Nicolle Atiliane Amorim de Farias
journal: Journal of voice : official journal of the Voice Foundation
abstract: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a non-invasive method to transiently adjust cortical excitability. Initial studies have reported changes in vocal parameters; however, it remains unclear whether tDCS can enhance the effects of structured vocal training. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the effects of sham stimulation with active tDCS using primary motor cortex (M1) or cerebellar electrode montages, when combined with vocal exercises in singers. Forty-five adult singers, without vocal symptoms or brain dysfunction, participated in this triple-blind randomized clinical trial. The participants underwent a 2-week intervention consisting of daily 20-minute tDCS sessions combined with a vocal exercise protocol, assigned to one of three groups: active anodal tDCS (2 mA) over either cerebellum or M1, or sham stimulation. All groups performed straw phonation in water (SPW). Voice recordings were taken before the intervention, after five and 10 sessions of intervention and at the follow-up (1 month after the intervention program) to assess the following vocal parameters: vocal range profile (VRP); vocal quality (jitter, shimmer, irregularity, glottal-to-noise excitation ratio - GNE, harmonic-to-noise ratio - HNR, smoothed cepstral peak prominence - CPPS and dysphonia acoustic index - DAI); Laryngeal neuromuscular control and coordination (Laryngeal diadochokinesis - LDDK), and self-reported vocal effort. Cerebellar anodal tDCS was associated with gains in VRP that were sustained over time, along with improvements in vocal quality during low-intensity phonation and an early reduction in perceived vocal effort compared with sham stimulation. In contrast, exploratory within-group changes were observed in the M1 group in high-intensity vocal quality (DAI), laryngeal coordination, and perceived vocal effort, without establishing an additional benefit over sham. Overall, superiority of active tDCS over sham during vocal training was not established, and the exploratory findings require confirmation.

title: Corrigendum to "MiR-143 enhances the antitumor activity of shikonin by targeting BAG3 expression in human glioblastoma stem cells" [Biochem. Biophys. Res. Commun., 468 (2015) 105-112].
Biomarker-led advances in renal cell carcinoma diagnosis, progression monitoring and therapeutic decision-making.
abstract: Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) diagnosis and management remain challenging due to asymptomatic presentation and limitations in accurately characterizing small renal masses. Noninvasive liquid biopsy biomarkers, including circulating proteins, metabolites, cell-free DNA, microRNAs, and inflammatory markers, have emerged as promising tools for RCC detection, prognostic stratification, and treatment monitoring. Here we review recent advances in blood- and urine-based biomarkers, highlighting key findings such as the diagnostic accuracy of kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1), CA15-3, metabolomic signatures, and urinary protein panels, alongside the prognostic relevance of circulating tumor DNA and systemic inflammatory indices. Despite encouraging analytical and clinical validity, no biomarker has yet demonstrated clinical utility due to biological, methodological, and regulatory challenges. Continued efforts focusing on standardized protocols, prospective validation, and integration with imaging and clinical data are essential to translate these biomarkers into personalized RCC management strategies.

title: Pyrimidine-based hybrids as modulators of P-glycoprotein-mediated multidrug resistance: lipophilicity and SAR perspectives.
abstract: An important obstacle to efficient anticancer therapy is multidrug resistance (MDR) mediated by efflux transporters, particularly P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1). Pyrimidine-based hybrids comprise different scaffolds with favorable physicochemical profiles that can modulate transporter activity. This review presents a descriptor-oriented analysis of the lipophilicity, polarity, amphiphilicity, and conformational flexibility across the principal structural architectures of pyrimidine hybrids (linked, fused, and natural product-derived), with conjugation considered as a cross-cutting structural feature to assess their influence on membrane permeability, intracellular accumulation, and P-gp modulation.Particular emphasis is placed on integrating experimentally determined and computationally predicted lipophilicity descriptors with structure-activity relationships (SAR) to demonstrate how scaffold architecture and physicochemical properties collectively influence MDR-related biological responses.This relationship is illustrated by studies on pyrimidine-hydrazone, pyrazolo[3,4-d]pyrimidine, oxazolo[5,4-d]pyrimidine, and artesunate-pyrimidine hybrids, which collectively demonstrate that balanced lipophilicity and amphiphilicity are key determinants of P-gp modulation.Collectively, SAR analyses, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and experimental studies indicate that hydrophobic and amphiphilic balance, rather than hydrogen-bonding capacity alone, govern P-gp recognition. By integrating structural, physicochemical, and biological findings, this review provides a framework for the rational optimization of pyrimidine-based hybrids to achieve more effective P-gp modulation and improved anticancer drug design.

title: From Rapid Synaptic Events to Lasting Antidepressant States: Convergent and Divergent Mechanisms of Ketamine and Psychedelics.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants have challenged the long-standing view that therapeutic improvement in major depressive disorder requires chronic treatment with monoaminergic agents. Ketamine and classical psychedelics act through distinct proximal targets, yet both can produce rapid and persistent behavioral effects that implicate synaptic and circuit plasticity as the core mechanisms of antidepressant action. This review, based on a minisymposium presented at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting, examines how brief pharmacological perturbations translate into lasting changes in mood-related networks. We first discuss hippocampal mechanisms underlying ketamine action, which include brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB)-dependent homeostatic potentiation, TrkB cross talk with metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) at CA3→CA1 synapses, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK)-dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6)-mediated extension of synaptic metaplasticity, and BDNF release at mossy fiber synapses and dentate gyrus neuronal maturation. We then consider how these local plasticity mechanisms interface with distributed circuits that regulate motivation, stress coping, and reward. Across brain regions, emerging work highlights the importance of cell type- and region-specific mechanisms that mediate ketamine's therapeutic actions. We expand on local prefrontal cortical inhibitory cellular signaling dynamics, including the interplay of various G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in cortical somatostatin interneurons and input-specific adaptations in accumbal circuits. Finally, we compare ketamine with psilocybin, an emerging therapeutic classic psychedelic for treatment-resistant depression that targets the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A (5-HT2A) receptor primarily. A recurring theme is that an interplay of GPCRs can help shape the timing, localization, and persistence of ketamine-induced neuroplasticity. Together, these studies suggest that antidepressant efficacy arises not from a single pathway or brain region but from coordinated, temporally staged plasticity across molecules, synapses, cells, and circuits.

title: Transforming Neuroscience Research through AI-Driven Data Integration and Analysis.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Integrating multimodal data is essential to advance neuroscience as a discipline. Large-scale collaborative efforts, exemplified by the BRAIN Initiative, together with advances in single-cell and spatial omics, multimodal imaging, human genetics, behavioral phenotyping, protein structure prediction, and related technologies, are transforming neuroscience into a data-rich, highly interconnected science. As experimental resources, scientific literature, and collaborative networks continue to expand, integrating discoveries across modalities, species, and levels of biological organization has become the field's central bottleneck. This Perspective argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming essential for overcoming these constraints. Using six evolving approaches we outline strategies to accelerate AI adoption through community building and pilot projects that drive AI transformation at both the organizational and technological levels. Organizational transformation cultivates broad AI awareness and a pro-AI culture while technological transformation improves the efficiency, scalability, and quality of data analysis, allowing researchers to generate insights more rapidly and effectively. Together, these advances position AI as a key driver for advancing neuroscience at scale.

title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Biophysical Mechanisms, Neural Effects, and Clinical Translation.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation technology capable of targeting both cortical and deep brain structures with millimeter-scale spatial precision. Recent advances in ultrasound hardware, acoustic modeling, neuronavigation, and multimodal imaging have accelerated the field from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward mechanistic investigation and early clinical translation. In parallel, growing evidence from animal and human studies has begun to clarify how ultrasound influences neural activity across cellular, circuit, and systems levels. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in understanding the biophysical mechanisms, neurophysiological effects, and network-level consequences of TUS. We discuss insights from optical imaging, electrophysiology, EEG source imaging, and functional MRI, highlighting how these complementary approaches reveal cell-type-specific responses, bidirectional modulation of neural circuits, and distributed changes in functional connectivity beyond the sonicated target. We further examine evidence that functional imaging is evolving from a simple measure of regional activation to a multidimensional biomarker of target engagement, circuit modulation, and treatment response. Despite these advances, important challenges remain. We conclude that TUS is approaching a translational inflection point in which rigorous mechanistic studies, standardized methodologies, and imaging-based biomarkers can establish ultrasound as both a powerful causal neuroscience tool and a clinically viable neuromodulation therapy for disorders involving dysfunctional brain circuits.

title: Placental-Neural Cross Talk: Biological Mechanisms Shaping Brain Architecture.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Impact of placental function on normal and pathological brain processes and supported behavior is an integrative research area dubbed "neuroplacentology." Placental functional genetics, structure, and vascular function have been discovered to have links to multiple clinical outcomes: autism, schizophrenia, and developmental cognitive impairment in offspring and postpartum depression and cognition in mothers. There are significant data showing that long-term impacts of preterm birth, diseases of pregnancy (preeclampsia), and maternal stress and depression may all be mediated by placental mechanisms, providing clinical and translational insights. Here, we will provide an up-to-date introduction to this emerging field. Mechanistic links between variations in placental structure and function and features of human and animal brain development and function will be discussed, clarifying basic biological connections and highlighting new targets to prevent clinical impairments.

title: Learning to Navigate a Changing World: From Brain Systems to Novel Algorithms.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Natural organisms navigate a world in constant flux and are frequently confronted with sensory ambiguity and shifting goals. While biological systems can adapt rapidly to navigate in novel and nonstationary environments, this challenge remains a significant hurdle for artificial intelligence. In this review, we examine recent progress in understanding neurobiological systems that allow for adaptive, efficient spatial and abstract navigation in dynamic environments and how these observations have informed new developments for the same behavior in machines. We highlight how predictive learning serves as a unifying framework to describe the organization of neural activity across distributed systems for navigation, including the hippocampal formation, parietal cortex, and higher-order associative structures. Specifically, we explore how such neurobiological systems encode expected future states, dynamic target trajectories, action plans, and internal behavioral strategies. Finally, we contrast the diffuse, inefficient exploration of canonical artificial agents with the structured, efficient control policies for goal-directed navigation observed in natural organisms. By grounding learning in the interplay between action, prediction, and natural behavioral statistics, navigation provides a roadmap for building resilient, neurobiologically inspired continual learning in artificial agents.

title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the "first-order" status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

title: Brain Initiative Roadmap: Building the Next Decade of NeuroAI.

title: Postnatal Development of Sensory Circuits Supporting Lifelong Social Behaviors.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Sensory systems are essential for young animals as they interact with their environments in order to survive and grow. These environments frequently involve other animals, especially early in life. Thus, animals' social interactions fundamentally shape and are shaped by their sensory circuit development. This Review and its associated Minisymposium will highlight new discoveries centered around the reciprocal relationship between sensory development and social interactions. Points of intersection range from gene expression in peripheral sensors to functional connectivity and neural coding in cortical circuits and span varied sensory systems and species. Taken together, we identify a common theme of refinement and specialization of sensory processing during limited developmental windows for species-relevant social behaviors. Consequently, early disruptions to sensory processing can have significant and long-lasting consequences for animals' lifelong behavior and may even contribute to the etiology of autism and related developmental disorders. Thus, the work presented herein offers mechanistic insight into the complex interplay between early sensory and social development with potentially significant clinical implications. Many of these insights are made possible by technological advances in measuring and manipulating sensory circuit functions and behaviors in developing animals. This Review aims to highlight recent advances and outstanding questions that lie at the nexus of sensory, social, and developmental neuroscience.

title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

title: Mu-Opioid Receptor in Habenula Circuits as a Substrate for Psychiatric Disorders and Addiction.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The habenula is a critical regulator of affect, negative reinforcement, avoidance, and coping behavior. It is thus unsurprising that accumulating evidence supports pivotal roles for habenular circuits in the expression of major psychiatric illnesses including depression and addiction. Though high levels of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) were identified in the habenula more than a generation ago, the functional effects of MORs on habenular circuits remained largely unexplored due to challenges of selectively targeting this small and heterogeneous brain structure. In this SfN mini-symposium report, we highlight studies that resolve how MOR is distributed across medial and lateral habenular subnuclei and how MOR expression maps onto molecularly defined habenular cell types. We further describe some of the habenula-intersecting circuits that express MORs and how MOR signaling modulates neural activity and neurotransmission within these unique habenular circuits and cell types. Going beyond cellular-level effects of MOR signaling, we illustrate how neural activity in the habenula can influence affect and behaviors associated with opioid analgesia, opioid seeking, opioid dependence, and opioid withdrawal. Drawing on works outside the opioid field, we suggest commonalities through which drugs of abuse may influence habenula circuits to induce states of negative affect that contribute to continued drug use or relapse. Finally, we discuss how better understanding the molecular and functional properties of habenular cell types and circuits can identify new druggable targets, such as the orphan receptors GPR151 and GPR139, for the treatment of pain, mood disorders, or opioid and other substance use disorders.

title: Cross-Species Approaches to Understanding Human Cognition.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Recent methodological advances including high-density intracranial recordings and population-level analytical frameworks enable deeper and more direct integration between animal models and human neuroscience. As a result, there is an increasing need for standardized behavioral paradigms and circuit-level analyses that can be used in both animals and humans. Cross-species approaches provide crucial foundations for treating neurological and psychiatric disorders. Parallel experiments validate therapeutic targets and enable development of mechanistically grounded behavioral biomarkers for early disease detection. Here, we provide a brief review of recent findings that have direct implications for attention deficits, memory impairments, and decision-making dysfunctions. By linking mechanism to behavior, these approaches guide targeted interventions and effective clinical translation. While challenges remain, these integrated approaches are advancing our understanding of the mechanistic foundation of human cognition.

title: Beyond Transcriptomes and Dissociated Cells: Spatial Proteomics for Mechanistic Neurobiology.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed remarkable molecular heterogeneity across neuronal and glial populations during development, aging, and disease. However, dissociation-based approaches disrupt tissue architecture, and RNA measures alone incompletely capture cellular function. These limitations are particularly relevant in neurodegenerative diseases, where pathology develops within cellular microenvironments and diseased cells progressively lose canonical cell-state identity markers. Spatial proteomic approaches are beginning to address this critical gap by enabling high-dimensional molecular profiling within the intact tissue, preserving the spatial relationships between vulnerable cells and their surrounding cellular environments across scales ranging from subcellular single-cell imaging to large-volume three-dimensional mapping. Here, we discuss emerging spatial proteomic technologies and their applications in aging and neurodegeneration, emphasizing how integration with complementary modalities, including transcriptomics, glycomics, three-dimensional genome architecture, and quantitative neuropathology, is providing new insight into disease biology. We further highlight how these approaches are beginning to accelerate therapeutic target validation, biomarker discovery, and treatment response monitoring. Realizing the full potential of spatial proteomics will require continued advances in cross-platform harmonization, analytical standardization, and computational methods capable of integrating increasingly complex, multimodal datasets.

title: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual Interoceptive-Exteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.

title: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.

title: Maternal Immune Activation and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Cross-Species Perspective.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Prenatal exposure to infection increases the likelihood of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). This association is attributed largely to the maternal inflammatory response, maternal immune activation (MIA), rather than to single pathogen. In this review, we discuss the molecular, cellular, and behavioral consequences of MIA and their contribution to NDDs in clinical cohorts and preclinical models across different species. We first trace the pathophysiology linking maternal infection to altered fetal neurodevelopment, describing how diverse immune challenges converge on shared nodes including cytokine signaling, oxidative and nutritional stress, placental dysfunction, and epigenetic modification. We then describe how these perturbations affect neural circuits and behavior, focusing on the disrupted social development. Next, we consider sources of individual variation, including gestational timing, fetal sex, and later-life "second hits," that may contribute to the greater vulnerability. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this work in terms of maternal cytokine and epigenetic signatures as candidate biomarkers for risk stratification and potential therapeutic approaches.

title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

title: NeuroAI's Next Steps: Balancing Computation and Embodiment.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Deep neural networks trained at scale now predict neural activity across sensory cortices, raising a question that divides neuroscience: does the convergence between artificial and biological representations constitute understanding, or does understanding require models of biological processes grounded in the embodied, evolved character of natural intelligence? In this Dual Perspectives article, Bing Brunton and Patrick Mineault articulate two research programs-Process and Convergence-to engage this question about the future of NeuroAI research. The conversation is organized around four questions that probe what scaled model-brain alignment reveals, what the brain is coupled to and evolved to do, what success beyond the lab looks like, and where the field should invest over the coming decade. Their exchanges reveal the distance between the two programs to be primarily about the level of analysis and priorities for what to build next. The conversation converges on shared ground: measure broadly, then distill to causal principles.

title: Hormonal Effects during the Reproductive Years on Brain and Behavior: Molecular Discovery to Promising Therapeutics for Women's Mental Health.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Beginning at puberty and throughout the lifespan, women experience greater rates of depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and hormone-linked mood disorders relative to men. How these disorders relate to hormonal fluctuations and associated changes in physiology and brain circuitry in women during the reproductive years is only partially understood. In this review, the molecular, structural, and functional brain changes during the reproductive years are discussed, with a specific focus on transitional changes during the perinatal period. Preclinical and clinical models of neuroplastic change are also discussed, along with neuromodulatory approaches that account for the contextual, spatial, and temporal parameters of interventions delivered during the postpartum period. Future directions may consider how hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years may improve preclinical and clinical models for women's mental health while acknowledging that greater work is needed to understand the role of a broader range of hormonal and environmental factors linked to mental health including lactation, trauma, contraceptive use, menstruation, and perimenopause.

title: The Noncanonical Hippocampus: Shared and Distinct Features of the CA2-FC-IG Hippocampal System.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The hippocampal CA2 region has received considerable interest in recent decades, earning a functional understanding beyond the previously held view as a small transitional zone. However, related hippocampal structures called the fasciola cinereum (FC) and indusium griseum (IG) have been largely neglected to date. While CA2, FC, and IG are typically presented as discontinuous structures on conventional atlases, recent work unveils a surprisingly high degree of overlapping gene expression and anatomical continuity, raising questions of their shared versus distinct functions. Here we review the molecular, anatomical, physiological, and behavioral features of each area, to begin to address whether these regions are subcomponents of a greater hippocampal structure or independent entities with distinct contributions to physiology and disease. Early evidence supports that the CA2-FC-IG axis is indeed a cohesive network unified by shared molecular and anatomical profiles, although regional differences in structure and function need to be taken into account. Notably, transcriptomics has revealed multiple subclusters within this complex of structures with no region-specific cell types, raising the need to understand whether cell types or anatomical subfields are the main functional units of this system. This conceptualization of these noncanonical hippocampal areas as a unified, multifaceted system raises many questions discussed here, along with the need for coordinated investigation across regions in future work.

title: Illuminating the Diversity of Electrical Synapse Form and Function.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: While the nervous system is organized by two main types of connections between neurons, electrical and chemical synapses, most studies focus upon the contribution of the molecularly complex and functionally diverse chemical synapse. Electrical synapses, in contrast, are perceived as simple, neuronal gap junction channels between contacts, often thought to be replaced in early development by more sophisticated chemical synapses. However, recent work and new tools push for the redefining of electrical synapse molecular architecture and function to allow for an updated interpretation of their ongoing contributions to neural circuit formation and function. Here, we describe fresh insight into neuronal gap junction structure, function, and molecular composition within invertebrate (nematodes, drosophila) and vertebrate (zebrafish, rabbit, rodent) model organisms across a variety of time periods and brain regions. Through molecular, genetic, connectomic, and functional explorations, our results argue for a new appreciation of electrical synapse heterogeneity. Based on these and other points of emerging new evidence, we argue for increased consideration of electrical synapses as complex and diverse structures which interact with chemical synapses to drive circuit formation and function.

title: Embodied Computation: How Does Embodiment Impact Sensorimotor and Cognitive Processing?
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Animals act on the world through a physical body and continually adjust behavior in response to the sensory feedback their actions produce. This closed loop between brain, body, and environment is central to motor control, but its role in other neural computations remains less clear. This review focuses on embodied computation: how the physical body shapes neural activity and behavior across functions ranging from motor control to cognitive processes. We examine the impact of embodiment in several domains, including compositional reuse, intrinsic motivation, metabolic costs, and connectome-constrained computation, with the broader aim of asking when the body can be abstracted away and when it is essential for explaining what the brain computes.

title: Glial Regulation of Motor Circuit Formation, Function, and Regeneration.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: From simple planaria to humans, proper assembly and maintenance of motor circuits is key to organismal survival. Each year, ∼250,000-500,000 individuals suffer a spinal cord injury with little hope of successful recovery. Moreover, motor circuits are a primary target of prevalent neurodegenerative conditions like ALS and Parkinson's disease. Thus, understanding the mechanisms that build, maintain, and rebuild motor circuits is of substantial clinical interest. Recent data indicate that glia, a heterogeneous group of non-neuronal cells within the nervous system, directly communicate with neurons to tune motor circuit dynamics. We now know glia are often active drivers of neural development and pathology, rather than passive bystanders. This mini-review will highlight recent advances in our understanding of how diverse glial cell types promote proper construction, function, and deconstruction of the key circuits that drive motor behavior.

title: The Neural Correlates of Sickness.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The brain protects animals during infection by detecting immune activity, coordinating behavioral and physiological defenses, anticipating potential infectious threats, and limiting excessive inflammation. Collectively termed sickness, these centrally organized responses include changes in body temperature, activity, energy balance, appetite, fluid intake, social behavior, neuroendocrine function, and autonomic output. Rather than constituting a single uniform state, sickness is generated by distributed and partially dissociable neural pathways that translate immune signals into responses appropriate to the nature and stage of an infection. Work presented at a symposium at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting highlights how humoral and cranial sensory pathways detect ongoing immune responses; how social cues, expectations, and prior experience prepare the organism for anticipated threats; and how endocrine and autonomic circuits constrain inflammation and promote recovery. Together, these findings establish the brain as an active regulator of immunity across the full course of illness.

title: Serotonin signaling in the rat prefrontal cortex is required for Retrieval-Induced Forgetting.
abstract: Forgetting is a ubiquitous phenomenon actively promoted in many species. The act of remembering some experiences can cause forgetting of others in both humans and rats. We previously found that when rats retrieve a memory to guide exploration, it reduces later retention of other competing memories encoded in that environment. As with humans, this retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF) relies on prefrontal control processes, is competition-dependent, and cue-independent. RIF is thought to be driven by inhibitory control signals from the prefrontal cortex that target areas where memories are stored. Serotonin plays a crucial role in behaviors requiring high cognitive demand, including memory processes, partly through its modulation of prefrontal cortex activity. However, its potential involvement in regulating active forgetting remains unexplored. Here, in male and female rats performing a task known to induce RIF, we pharmacologically manipulated serotonin 5-HT1A, 5-HT2A, and 5-HT2C receptors and their downstream effectors in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). Our findings reveal a specific role for prefrontal serotonin signaling in RIF. Whereas 5-HT2C receptor manipulation had no effect, activating 5-HT1A or blocking 5-HT2A receptors in the mPFC abolished RIF. By contrast, activating 5-HT2A receptors promotes RIF under conditions in which it is normally reduced. Further analyses identified the PI3K/AKT pathway as a downstream effector of 5-HT2A receptor signaling, suggesting a specific molecular mechanism through which serotonin modulates inhibitory control over memory. These results uncover a previously unrecognized serotonergic modulation of adaptive forgetting, identifying specific receptor subtypes that link prefrontal serotonin signaling to inhibitory control over memory competition.Significance statement Forgetting is an essential, active process that helps the brain stay flexible and focused. In both humans and animals, remembering one thing can lead to forgetting competing memories, a phenomenon called retrieval-induced forgetting (RIF). Our research shows that serotonin, a neurotransmitter best known for its role in mood, also actively regulates which memories are forgotten. In rats, we found that serotonin signaling in the prefrontal cortex regulates adaptive forgetting: 5-HT2A receptor signaling promotes RIF, whereas activation of 5-HT1A receptors disrupts it. We further identified PI3K/AKT signaling as a key downstream effector of 5-HT2A receptor activation in this process. These findings matter because the mechanisms of active forgetting remain poorly understood, and their disruption may contribute to psychopathological conditions.

title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD.Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning.Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

title: Characterization of the 3D Structure of Chromatin in D1 and D2 Medium Spiny Neurons of the Nucleus Accumbens.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: The 3D structure of chromatin is tightly regulated in concert with cell differentiation during development and with epigenetic regulation of gene expression throughout life. Despite extensive characterization at the transcriptional and epigenetic levels of D1-type and D2-type medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) - the ventral portion of the striatum important for reward - a 3D map of chromatin structure in these two neuronal cell types is lacking. Here, we provide a high-density map of chromatin structure from male mice in D1 and D2 MSNs including chromatin loops, topological associating domains (TADs), sub-TADs, and compartments. The data suggest broad convergence in overall 3D chromatin structure between these two closely aligned cell types, but also clear differences consistent with transcriptional divergence previously demonstrated for the two MSN types. We also demonstrate that various exposures to cocaine (acute, chronic, or chronic + acute) - which dramatically alter transcriptional patterns in NAc MSNs - produce far more subtle changes in 3D chromatin structure. Thus, while the 3D structure of chromatin in NAc MSNs appears to be an important concomitant of cell type, it is not broadly leveraged by cocaine to mediate changes in gene expression that contribute to a state of addiction.Significance Statement D1-type and D2-type subtypes of medium spiny neurons are present in the nucleus accumbens and perform different roles in drug addiction. This study maps the genome-wide 3D structure of chromatin in the neuronal subtypes and examines how chronic cocaine exposure alters the chromatin landscape of D1 and D2 MSNs.

title: Neural Responses to Unexpected Stimulus Repetitions and Omissions in Auditory Cortex Provide Mixed Evidence for Predictive Coding.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Humans and other animals process sensory uncertainty by integrating stimulus information with prior knowledge and expectations. Predictive coding conceptualizes perception as a form of Bayesian inference wherein hierarchical brain circuits update internal models to reconcile bottom-up sensory input with top-down predictions. Whereas predictive coding is a leading theory, the extent to which it is implemented in primary sensory cortices remains a matter of debate. To further investigate this issue, we examined single-neuron spiking activity in male macaque primary auditory cortex (A1) to expected versus unexpected stimulus repetitions and to expected versus unexpected stimulus omissions. On average, we found that A1 neurons did not show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus repetitions, contrary to predictive-coding theory. However, they did show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus omissions. Taken together, these mixed results place empirical constraints on how predictive coding is implemented in A1.Significance Statement Perception depends on the brain's ability to infer the causes of sensory inputs by integrating new information with prior knowledge under uncertainty. Our results reveal nuanced evidence for predictive coding within the primary auditory cortex (A1). Specifically, spiking activity during unexpected stimuli and unexpected stimulus omissions provide conflicting and supporting data, respectively, for this Bayesian framework. These findings refine our understanding of neural mechanisms underlying perception and provide empirical constraints on the neurobiological implementation of predictive processing.

title: Different lineages, one fate: convergent astrocyte differentiation in C. elegans.
abstract: Astrocytes arise from molecularly distinct progenitors, yet how these lineages converge on a common glial identity remains unclear. In this issue of Genes & Development, Liu and colleagues (doi:10.1101/gad.353618.125) dissect this process in Caenorhabditis elegans CEPsh glia, which parallel functionally mammalian radial glia and its transition to astrocytes. CEPsh progenitors converge transcriptionally before postmitotic maturation. The CEH-43/Distal-less transcription factor acts as a terminal selector, directly regulating both the convergent embryonic program and the subsequent acquisition of mature astrocyte-like features. Comparative transcriptomics shows molecular similarities between CEPsh glia and mammalian astrocytes. These findings reveal a regulatory logic for convergent differentiation that could apply to other contexts.

title: Ideal MIGS trial: linking design to robust outcomes.

Exclude or expose in irritable bowel syndrome study: what works for whom and how? Protocol for a randomised controlled trial of internet-delivered FODMAP diet versus exposure-based cognitive behavioural therapy.
From intracellular force maps to organelle and organism physiology.
abstract: The mechanical properties of the cell interior are heterogeneous, varying across components and compartments according to function, location and time. However, many current mechanical models of the cell do not fully reflect this, either treating the cell as a simplified isotropic mechanical continuum or focusing on complex mechanics of isolated cellular structures, leaving the integration of mechanical features at cellular-to-tissue levels unresolved. To link mechanics with biological function, complete, spatially and temporally resolved maps of subcellular to mesoscopic mechanical properties in living systems and organisms are needed. Despite major technical advances in mechanobiology over the past decade, only snapshots of these heterogenous material properties have been obtained. Crucially, the integration of quantitative force measurements with microscopy approaches remains a challenge in connecting cell mechanics with biological structure and function. This limitation underlines the urgent need for novel imaging methods to visualize how different organelles, cells and organisms respond to forces and how their mechanical properties are coupled to function and physiology.
